children.text: The very edge of-- I grew up, well, in different places. I have in those photographs that my wife dug up. I have photographs of the house where I was born. It's on Van Buren between 14th and 15th. They used to build them well in those days. It's still inhabited apparently.

Lorenzo, my brother, had one of his grandsons take those pictures. Now, I don't remember anything about that house. Though apparently, we lived there from about 1904 to 1915. I was born there, then we moved to the edge of town because my father had decided he wanted more room.
He grew up on a ranch, but he wanted to become a farmer.
Do you still feel you have a bond with Brownsville?

As I said, emotionally, yes. It'll always be my hometown but I recognize it less and less. For example, that house is still standing. But the house where we lived and which I used as a background for George Washington Gómez's early days, no longer exists and that area has deteriorated against--

Because waves of new immigrants, fleeing the economic conditions in Mexico have moved into that area for the most part. We moved back to 14th street, which was a main artery then. It was paved, it was a two-lane but it went to Point Isabel. Now it's called Port Isabel.

La Punta Isabel and Boca Chica and to Los Fresnos and different places. We moved back at that time on 14th street. As a young man I had, of course, a lot of barrio [neighborhood] friends but most of them moved away and I moved away from them too.

They dropped out of school very early, some of them never got a chance to go to school. One of them herded goats instead, though his father had a dairy. He was the one that was born in the house next to ours, on the same date that I was born.

Yet sometimes when he had grown, he would look me up and said, "Américo, ¿cuántos años tenemos?" [How old are we?] [laughs] He didn't even know how old he was. My friends became from farther away from school.
Dr. Paredes, I don't have any more questions. If there's anything else you'd like to say. Maybe we haven't touched on or Dr. Medrano hasn't touched on.
Remember the number of the house, Dr. Paredes? Because we were planning on going there and maybe shoot it.

That photograph- on the back. Lorenzo, my surviving brother, would be 91 by the way in October. He went to the house, of course that was a number of years ago with one of his grandsons and they took pictures and in the back he wrote exactly the number of the house. You might want to see those pictures in a minute.
Anything else you'd like to say or that we haven't touched on?

Only that I did develop bilingually because in junior high, more and more of my classmates were Anglos. Outside when we were in the playground, I played with Mexicans, but in junior high a very strange thing happened. Three Anglos and I were put in a class, there were only those four of us.

The class was about Ancient History. I enjoyed that class. I remember the names of the three. I remember the name of the teacher, Ms. Bell. These things happened, they wouldn't believe. Once a man called me, he was a traveling salesman and told me, "My wife was your teacher, Allie Bell."

I didn't even know her first name. I mentioned that I would like to meet her. The next time he came and told me that she died. I never knew why we four were chosen for what nowadays would be, I suppose, a culture enrichment course.

The other three, one was named Bolin, the other Beeson and Abbott was the other one. In class, we were very close friends. But after class, in weekends they would come back on Monday and talk about what they had done, how they had visited. That part I was included. I began to develop my own group.

I really began to live in two worlds. Began to have more in... In junior college most of my friends, except for those three [inaudible] were Anglos. My older son of the present wife had as a teacher, the wife of one of my schoolmates in junior college. His name was Don Irwin.

In fact, we had been pretty close together again. In the building, I had even written some little skits under the name of Washington Gómez. Then I found out that it was his wife that was teaching here. I called him once about having coffee together, he said he was too busy.

Then, not long after that, he died. In Brownsville, Bruce Underwood, I know whether you know. I haven't been able to get in touch with him because of my infernal problem with names. I went out there looking for him and I confused him with Bruce Aiken. Bruce Aiken I knew his father quite well.
He was not Bruce Underwood. [laughs] I don't know what became of Bruce. Is he still there?
Bruce, yes. Bruce Aiken is still there. Bruce Underwood sounds familiar. Who is he?
I've heard the name before and I always jot it down but I don't know where he is.
First, he worked for The Herald , I think. Then he had a little weekly, I think. I think he's still around there.
I think he is, but I don't know exactly where to contact him.

The thing is that when we do-- [video cut] -Mainly to see Lorenzo and Amador's widow, and probably go across. I don't even go across the border anymore. I'm afraid of those guys now. [laughs] Did you read that the president Zedillo's son was almost mugged by three policemen?

Sí, policemen. They stopped them and they started the mugging, but behind was a car full of his bodyguards [laughs] and they come up with to arrest the three police. North Mexico, poor Mexico is in very bad shape.
I have one more question for you. If you were speaking to a group of students in Brownsville today, what would you say about the importance of being bilingual? Why is that so important?

tags.tag: The Institutional Revolutionary Party--Partido Revolucionario Institucional

children.text: It's very important. It will be more important if the Mexican Government gets its act together or the PRI is booted out, which I doubt very much. NAFTA really starts working. I really am sorry that more of our young people are completely forgetting their Spanish.

tags.tag: The Institutional Revolutionary Party--Partido Revolucionario Institucional

children.text: They're missing a lot of opportunities there. I would include my own two sons, the ones from this-- Because they were raised in a purely Anglo environment. I remember with Alan, you may see his pictures in a while. I tried to teach him Spanish, I would talk all in Spanish

tags.tag: The Institutional Revolutionary Party--Partido Revolucionario Institucional

children.text: and he would answer in English. Finally, in English I told him, "Why don't you speak to me in Spanish?". He was probably three years old. He said, "Daddy, Spanish is for grown-ups, kids talk English." [laughs] Which really was the case because all his friends in school--

tags.tag: The Institutional Revolutionary Party--Partido Revolucionario Institucional

children.text: This was not our town so we didn't move to East Austin. We moved where faculty people lived and none of them spoke Spanish.

tags.tag: The Institutional Revolutionary Party--Partido Revolucionario Institucional

children.text: I remember kids getting in trouble for speaking Spanish on the playground.

tags.tag: The Institutional Revolutionary Party--Partido Revolucionario Institucional

children.text: Yes, not in my time because there were too many of us I think, but later I remember-- Manfredo, you were talking about Manfredo? When he was assistant principal at the Putegnat, we stopped by to say goodbye to him. He was on the playground and he came over, he had a big paddle like that.

tags.tag: The Institutional Revolutionary Party--Partido Revolucionario Institucional

children.text: I was speaking Spanish to him and said, "¿Para qué es eso?" [What is that for?]. "Para pegarles a los huercos." [To hit the kids.] He had paddled them because they spoke Spanish [laughs] and there he was speaking Spanish to me, it didn't make sense. That's the practical thing.

tags.tag: The Institutional Revolutionary Party--Partido Revolucionario Institucional

children.text: The other thing is that knowing two languages, two cultures, two literatures, you are a double person. There's a great deal more to you and it's quite possible. I had another very dear friend of mine that died about a year ago, he was born in Germany. He had a very strange name,

tags.tag: de la Croix, Horst Maximilian Albert

children.text: His name was Horst Maximilian Albert de la Croix, the last name was French.

tags.tag: de la Croix, Horst Maximilian Albert

children.text: Pretty name.

tags.tag: de la Croix, Horst Maximilian Albert

children.text: He was a descendant of French Huguenots who had fled from France and settled in Prussia, his father had been a Prussian officer in World War I. But he could speak Spanish, of course his own German. Spanish, English, and French, besides German. When we were in Japan he picked up Japanese like that,

tags.tag: de la Croix, Horst Maximilian Albert

children.text: much faster than I did, so his world was much bigger than even mine was. Knowing two languages, two cultures, is very important, and very often that's something that-- I visited a class a few days ago and that came up also. There's a man who is no longer young, Richard Rodriguez, Hunger of Memory,

tags.tag: de la Croix, Horst Maximilian Albert

children.text: is that, who was- rejected his background. In the class as a teacher was a young man in history here whose name is Neil Foley but his father was an Irish, though he still lives. He was a professor of Spanish, his mother was Mexican. Now, he not only lives in two cultures but his genes participate.

tags.tag: de la Croix, Horst Maximilian Albert

children.text: Then Rolando Hinojosa, a very dear friend, his mother was an Anglo but, again, she knew Spanish and he grew in a Mexican neighborhood in Mercedes, so he can be two people. I've noticed that sometimes in the hall I would hear him talking to an Anglo and he sounded exactly like an Anglo.

tags.tag: de la Croix, Horst Maximilian Albert

children.text: Then he would come and talk to me and he was a Mexican, [laughs] but that didn't give him any complexes. You get those complexes if you're not sure of yourself I think.

tags.tag: de la Croix, Horst Maximilian Albert

children.text: Thank you very much. [Letty: Thank you.]

tags.tag: de la Croix, Horst Maximilian Albert

children.text: May we go to your study, Dr. Paredes, to take some photographs? Would that be all right with you?
Yes, or if you want to see those photographs I bring them here, you might want-

[crosstalk] Let's take your microphone off -Yes, you can videotape the photographs while we-- What we can do is we can videotape the photographs of Dr. Paredes and then they're going to take some photographs of you.
First, let's see-
You're going to tell us a little bit about each of the photographs.
If you show me the ones you want.
The best thing to do is let him talk to us about the photographs that we have--
Let me bring the photographs.
Great, thank you.
[background conversation] [video cut]
[On screen: Black and white photo of Americo with his wife, three sons, and a daughter-in-law. Americo is holding his NEH Award.]
Because I don't remember what this was about anymore.
That's the award that's back there.
Yes.
Do you want me to bring it?
Would you mind? Because I think the NEH-- [crosstalk]
This is your family, right? Your wife and your three sons?
That's my wife, my three sons, and one daughter-in-law. [background noise]
I think this is the one in that picture.
Yes, all I remember is that I think I got $5,000 worth it. Yes, the National Endowment for the Humanities, the Charles Frankel Award.
Yes, this is it. [?] . [background conversation] [background noise]
Yes, I think he's got that over there. I think here, this is his parents.
[On screen: Black and white photo of Americo with his NEH Award.]
Yes, definitely that one. -That's the Frankel.
Yes, but the NEH was the one that gave the award, the Frankel.
That was the first time they gave it.
Really? That was his first recipient for that award?
Yes.
There were four people but it was--
Four people in the United States.
Always thinking of tokenism I thought that one of the other four was going to be black but it wasn't the case. [laughter] [background conversation]
This was a photograph that was used for With His Pistol in His Hand, I think.

tags.tag: With His Pistol in His Hand
With His Pistol in His Hand

children.text: For the dust jacket of With His Pistol in His Hand.

tags.tag: With His Pistol in His Hand

children.text: That was taken in 1958, or around that time period?

tags.tag: With His Pistol in His Hand

children.text: [On screen: Black and white portrait of a young Americo Paredes with a guitar.]

tags.tag: With His Pistol in His Hand

children.text: Probably 1956-57. That old guitar I had it since before World War II.

tags.tag: With His Pistol in His Hand

children.text: Mary Murphy. [chuckles]

tags.tag: With His Pistol in His Hand

children.text: I could play the thing in those days.

tags.tag: With His Pistol in His Hand

children.text: Can you still play it? I bet you can.

tags.tag: With His Pistol in His Hand

children.text: No, I haven't, see my fingers and I don't have the time for it. I used to play the piano so, this piano isn't mine. I used to sing also, you think I want to sing? [laughs]

tags.tag: With His Pistol in His Hand

children.text: My mami used to listen to you on the radio, mi mamá lo escuchaba.

tags.tag: With His Pistol in His Hand

children.text: Now those days are gone forever.

tags.tag: With His Pistol in His Hand

children.text: What was the radio station?
He didn't remember the name, I think it might have been the old KBOR. I think he said the 1930s, is that correct, Dr. Paredes?
Yes.
In the 1950s it was KBOR in Brownsville. It might have been, right?
Where was KBOR?
KBOR was on Central Boulevard.

No, I think that was the station in which José Cantú used to be. Have you heard of José Cantú? He was a really strong social critic. He died in an accident but we believe that he was killed, it wasn't an accident. He was very critical of Juan N. Guerra

who was the uncle of this big shot in the drug business now. But he used to end it with a little phrase- His wife was named María de Jesús, "¿Me estás oyendo, chucha?" ["Are you listening to me Chucha?"]. [laughter]
All the people used to love him.
I bet he was popular. [crosstalk]

I think they were recorded, but that's where that station was. This one that where I used to sing that may have been Central-- Now, if you're coming down Elizabeth, or up Elizabeth, going north more or less, then you used to reach a point where it was a dead end, you turned into a highway.
[On screen: Black and white photo of Americo Paredes' parents, Justo and Clotilde Paredes.]
Yes, that's KBOR. -Yes, that's KBOR, it's an old white stucco with a red towel rig on.
Later it would've been on the left.
Because it ends and then that was the old highway.
Yes, the military highway, that's where west Brownsville is.
It was on the military highway. Yes, that's where it was.
That's his parents. This is your parents, right? [Americo: Yes]
That was taken in 1914, correct?

1914, in fact, he gave that to a sister-in-law. In fact, the wife of my uncle, Vicente, and it's faded, but you can see the writing, apparently, when she died. I don't know how Lorenzo got hold of it, and he gave it to me.
No, KBOR isn't there anymore, it's a bank.
What is the name of it? KB?
KBOR. B.
B. -B-O-R.
They used to do the birthday book, that's what I remember about it. Every morning, they'd have the birthday book.
That's it. Of course, we didn't call it the Central Boulevard then. It was a highway there. -When did it close?
[On screen: The back of the photo of Americos' parents, it appears to have handwriting by Justo Paredes.]
It's still up, it's still on the air, but it's in another building, but it left that.
I think it's a mortgage company building, but they're still broadcasting.
Bruce Aiken wrote the-- [video cut] -There were several other people, he was in the front passenger seat, and he was the only one that was hurt.
[On screen: A color photo of a young Americo Paredes and two other men on horseback.]
Was that in Boca Chica? On the way out of the- on that road?

Yes, they were coming back. There were a lot of people that didn't like him, especially in Matamoros, Juan N. Guerra and others. In the beginning, there were real border mafia there. Now, I understand it's the nephew of Juan N. Guerra.
He used to be the mayor. He was recently the mayor.
Garcia, I think, I forgot his name.
What was his name? The former mayor.
Juan N. Guerra. There was his nephew, and he was the mayor maybe three terms ago .
Yes, I remember. -Remember he would feed the pigeons? Remember them? -I remember them. [background noise]
[On screen, continuous: A color photo of a young Americo Paredes and two other men on horseback.]
I was doing fieldwork in Durango, Pancho Villa's stomping ground. That's me over on the right. Up in the mountains. [Manuel: You were doing some research?]
I used to do a lot of fieldwork, collecting songs. I think on that trip, I was collecting jokes.
[video cuts to black]
